body_html:
Update:

  • Aug10’26: Q3 2026 Earnings Results & Revised target ($126 (split adj.) → $120)

As I mentioned a couple of weeks ago, while less than 20% of the positions are in the AI-theme, it represents 40% of the portfolio value due to the gains in those positions. And also I am getting a bit burnt out of reading, analysing, talking AI, so I am switching to another sector that I love and that would help the portfolio diversification and keep me sane…financials.

Most people who glance at this company see a +$100B revenue business that earns a wafer-thin margin and assume it’s a low-quality commodity reseller. They stop reading there. That is the mispricing. Almost all of that +$100B is the pass-through cost of physical commodities it moves for clients. The number that actually matters, net operating revenue, is compounding at 20% a year. On that real top line it earns a 20%-plus pre-tax margin and, in the last two quarters, a ROE north of 22%. The market is paying about $9B for the whole thing.

Here is the part that made me sit up. In the first half of this fiscal year alone, the business earned $313M of net income, more than it booked in the whole of the prior year. Run that pace for a full year and you have a company throwing off well over $600M of cash against a $9B price tag. For a capital-light intermediary where accounting earnings and free cash flow sit close together, that is a free-cash-flow yield few people would ever pin on a name that screens as a thin-margin commodity trader.

So the question is simple. Is this a volatility-juiced one-off that just had two lucky quarters, or a genuine compounder that the market still misreads because of how its revenue is presented? I think it’s the second, and the cash flow against the price is the cleanest way to see it.

I sent this pick to paid subscribers as a real-time trade alert on 10 June…

… and it is already up 8.3%.

Upgrade to paid to unlock the full deep dive, plus every future pick and trade alert the moment I send it.

Table of Contents

  • TLDR

  • How the company actually makes money

  • Industry structure: the middle-market gap

  • The volatility engine, and why it’s a feature

  • The four segments

  • Acquisitions and the consolidation tailwind

  • What the market is paying: free cash flow against a $9B price

  • Scenario analysis: discount rate and growth

  • Financials and the DCF

  • The bear case

  • Variant perception

  • Verdict

TLDR

  • StoneX is a middle-market capital markets intermediary. It connects farmers, corporates, asset managers, hedge funds and retail traders to exchanges and OTC markets, earning spreads, fees, and interest on client cash. The figure that matters is net operating revenue of $2.05B in FY2025, the number the $131B gross line hides.

  • The bull case rests on three things: structural growth as banks retreat from the middle market, a 20%-plus ROE that compounds retained capital, and earnings that rise when markets get volatile. Net operating revenue has grown roughly 19% a year for five years through both calm and chaos.

  • The free-cash-flow story is the anchor. H1 FY2026 net income of $313M already tops all of FY2025. On the current run-rate the business earns north of $600M, a roughly 6.5% to 7% cash yield on a $9B market cap, and it’s still growing.

  • The key risk is honest and real. A large slice of recent earnings is volatility-driven. Normalize volatility, cut rates, and earnings fall toward mid-cycle. My bear DCF lands at about $80, roughly 30% below today’s $116.

  • My updated DCF base case is about $190 a share, near 64% above the current price, on assumptions at or below StoneX’s own recent results. The valuation leans on a low discount rate and a high through-cycle return on equity, so treat the base as the optimistic end of a wide range, not a point estimate.

This is a business most people find boring right up until they look at what it earns. Below is how it actually works, why the cash flow is the tell, and what would have to go wrong.

How the company actually makes money

Strip away the jargon and StoneX is a toll booth on the plumbing of global markets. A grain elevator in Iowa that needs to hedge next season’s corn, a mid-sized asset manager that wants to clear and custody securities, a company in Kenya that needs to pay a supplier in a currency its bank won’t touch, a retail trader who wants to short the euro at two in the morning. None of these clients is large enough for a bulge-bracket bank to bother with at a sensible price. StoneX sits in that gap and charges a small toll on each transaction, position, and balance.

Three things drive the real top line.

The first is spreads. When StoneX executes or makes a market in a futures contract, an FX pair, or a physical metal, it captures the difference between what it buys and sells at.

The second is fees, charged for clearing, custody, consulting, and account services.

The third is interest earned on client float, the cash clients park with StoneX as margin and settlement balances. In a higher-rate world that float income is real money, and it shows up in net operating revenue rather than as a financing footnote.

The accounting is where most people get lost, so it’s worth being precise. StoneX reports gross revenue of around $131B because it books the full value of the physical commodities it sells. Almost all of that is offset immediately by the cost of those commodities. Strip out the cost of physical commodities and you get what management calls operating revenue, around $4.1B last year. That is far better than the gross line, yet it still carries the transactional costs that come straight off the top: transaction-based clearing, introducing-broker commissions, and interest expense. Take those out too and you reach net operating revenue. Net operating revenue is the right anchor because the items sitting between operating revenue and net operating revenue are pass-through costs that scale almost one-for-one with the volume booked above them, so they reveal nothing about the firm’s own economics. Operating revenue still flatters the picture, net operating revenue strips it back to what StoneX actually keeps to run itself. That is the number management runs the company on, the number analysts should anchor to, and the number that grew from $868M in FY2020 to $2.05B in FY2025. Anyone valuing StoneX off the gross line is solving the wrong problem.

Once you frame it on net operating revenue, the economics get clear. Compensation and benefits run a little over half of net operating revenue, the largest single cost because this is a people-and-technology business rather than a capital-heavy one. Non-compensation costs, technology, professional fees, occupancy, shared services, run another quarter or so. What falls through is pre-tax operating income, about 20% of net operating revenue in FY2025 and climbing as the business scales. There is almost no inventory, the capital expenditure is light, and depreciation roughly matches it. That combination, a 20%-plus pre-tax margin on a fast-growing real top line with little reinvestment in fixed assets, is what makes the cash flow so good.

Industry structure: the middle-market gap

The reason StoneX exists, and the reason it keeps growing, is a gap that regulation widened and is not closing. After the financial crisis, capital rules made it expensive for large banks to hold inventory, clear smaller clients, and warehouse risk for accounts that don’t move the needle on a trillion-dollar balance sheet. So the banks walked away from the middle. They kept the mega-corporates and the largest institutions and quietly stopped serving the grain co-op, the regional asset manager, the frontier-market importer. Those clients didn’t stop needing market access. They just lost their supplier.

StoneX is the company that picked up the orphaned middle. It now serves more than 50,000 institutional and commercial clients and over 250,000 self-directed accounts, giving them access to upwards of 40 exchanges, roughly 18,000 OTC products, and more than a hundred currency pairs through a single platform. That breadth is the moat. A new entrant can copy one product line, but replicating the full lifecycle, advice, execution, clearing, custody, and payments, across every asset class and 180-plus countries, takes decades and a balance sheet that can carry the risk. StoneX has spent a century and dozens of acquisitions building exactly that.

The second structural force is consolidation. The non-bank brokerage world is fragmenting and re-aggregating at the same time. Small futures commission merchants and regional brokers struggle with the cost of compliance, technology, and capital, so they sell. StoneX is the natural buyer, and each deal adds clients and cleared volume to the same fixed infrastructure. Scale in this business is a compounding advantage: more volume over the same platform lowers unit cost, funds better technology, and makes the next acquisition more accretive. The RJO deal, which made StoneX the largest non-bank futures commission merchant in the United States, is consolidation working in StoneX’s favour. The middle-market gap is the demand. Consolidation is the supply-side mechanism by which StoneX keeps taking share of it.

The volatility engine, and why it’s a feature

Here is the trait that scares people and shouldn’t. StoneX earns more when markets get violent. When volatility spikes, spreads widen and clients trade and hedge more often. A farmer hedges more aggressively when grain prices whipsaw. A corporate treasury reaches for cover when its currency lurches. A hedge fund churns more when the tape moves. Every one of those reactions is a transaction StoneX clears and a spread it captures.

The track record backs this up. StoneX’s business boomed through the pandemic shock of 2020 and again through the 2022 rate-hiking and commodity dislocation. The most recent two quarters are the clearest proof yet. In Q1 FY2026 net operating revenue rose 47% y/y to a record $724.4M and net income hit $139M. In Q2 FY2026, the quarter ended 31 March, net operating revenue jumped 70% y/y to a record $829.1M, net income reached a record $174.3M, diluted EPS was $2.07, and return on equity ran at 26.5%. Adjusted EBITDA more than doubled. That is what operating leverage looks like when volume surges across a fixed cost base.

Most people treat this as a flaw, low-quality earnings that will mean-revert. I read it differently. A business that earns more precisely when the rest of a portfolio is hurting is doing something rare. It is a hedge that also compounds. In a calm year StoneX still grows net operating revenue through new clients, new products, and float income. In a chaotic year it prints. You don’t often get an asset that pays you to hold it through the quiet stretches and then pays you again when everything else is on fire. The cyclicality is real, but framing it purely as a weakness misses why it belongs in a portfolio in the first place.

The honest caveat, which I’ll come back to in the bear case, is that you cannot capitalize a 26% ROE quarter as if it were forever. The right way to think about StoneX is mid-cycle earnings power first, with volatility as a free option layered on top.

The four segments

StoneX runs four operating segments, and understanding the mix tells you where the durability sits.

Commercial is the heart of the moat. This is risk management and hedging for farmers, food companies, energy producers, and metals businesses, plus the physical trading of commodities like grains and precious metals. It generated $1.1B of net operating revenue in TTM Q2 2026. What protects it is service depth. StoneX walks a client through the entire lifecycle of a hedge, high-touch advice plus electronic execution and clearing, for customers that no large bank will hold by the hand. That is sticky, relationship-driven revenue that doesn’t churn on price alone.

Institutional is now the growth engine and the largest segment at $1.1B of net operating revenue in TTM Q2 2026. It serves asset managers and financial institutions with securities trading, prime brokerage, clearing, research, and custody. This is where the listed-derivatives and securities volumes scaled hardest in FY2026, and where the recent acquisition adds the most.

Self-Directed/Retail is FX and CFD trading for retail customers through the FOREX.com and City Index platforms. It’s smaller and more cyclical, but it carries high incremental margins when retail engagement rises.

Payments is the quiet gem. StoneX moves cross-border payments in local currency to more than 180 countries and over 140 currencies, mostly for banks and corporates paying into hard-to-reach markets. It is capital-light, high-margin, recurring, and structurally growing as global commerce reaches further into frontier markets. If the rest of StoneX is a volatility play, Payments is the annuity underneath it.

The point of the segment map is balance. No single segment is more than about 40% of the real top line. Commercial is the durable relationship base, Institutional is the scale and growth, Payments is the annuity, Retail is the high-octane option. The diversification is why net operating revenue has compounded so steadily even as any one driver zigzags.

Acquisitions and the consolidation tailwind

StoneX has grown through bolt-on acquisitions for decades.

The most important recent move is the purchase of R.J. O’Brien, the oldest futures brokerage in the US. The deal was for $900M of equity value, $625M in cash plus about 3.5 million StoneX shares, and assumed up to $143M of RJO debt, pushing the all-in price above $1B. It closed on 31 July 2025.

The strategic logic is straightforward. RJO makes StoneX the largest non-bank futures commission merchant in the US. It brings a deep book of introducing brokers and commercial clients, more cleared volume across the same fixed infrastructure, and a wider cross-sell surface for StoneX’s hedging, payments, and securities services. Management targets $100M of annual cost and revenue benefits within two years. Treat that figure as a management claim until the integration proves it, but the direction is right. This is a scale business, and bolting a century-old client franchise onto StoneX’s platform is the right type of acquisition in my opinion.

The long record is what earns management the benefit of the doubt. StoneX traces its roots to Saul Stone in the 1920s, and over the past decades, the stock has delivered a compound annual return north of 30%, built on a steady cadence of bolt-on deals layered on top of organic growth.

That is not a promotional management team chasing a story. It is an operating team that has quietly turned a micro-cap broker into a global platform by buying franchises at sensible prices and integrating them onto shared infrastructure.

The capital allocation around RJO fits the pattern. StoneX funded most of the deal with cash and a modest share issue rather than blowing out the balance sheet. It also raised its buyback authorization for FY2026 to up to 2.25 million shares, from 1.5 million the year before, roughly 3% of the share base. Management compensation is tied to a 15% ROE target, and the company has consistently cleared it.

That is the profile I want in a serial acquirer: a real return hurdle, skin in the game, and a track record of deals that compound rather than dilute.

What the market is paying: free cash flow against a $9B price

This is the centre of the thesis, so I’ll be precise about the cash.

For an intermediary like StoneX, reported operating cash flow is close to useless on its own. It swings by billions from quarter to quarter as client and segregated balances move in and out. Those flows are client float, money that belongs to customers and washes straight through. The clean way to measure FCF here is net income, because capex runs close to depreciation, there is no inventory build to fund, and working capital is client float that nets out. Net income slightly understates cash, if anything, because depreciation and amortization, lifted by acquired intangibles, runs ahead of the cash StoneX spends on equipment and software. So net income is a fair-to-conservative proxy for the cash this business generates for its owners. This is the orthodox way to value a financial intermediary. Aswath Damodaran makes the case directly in Valuing Financial Service Firms: for banks and brokers, debt is closer to raw material than to financing, so you value the equity straight off cash flow to equity, and you treat the regulatory and balance-sheet capital the firm must retain to grow as its true reinvestment. That is exactly what the model does, which is why I discount free cash flow to equity at the cost of equity and net out the capital StoneX keeps back to fund its growth, rather than running a standard enterprise-value bridge that the client float would distort.

Now line that up against the roughly $9B the market is asking.

In FY2025, a year of merely normal volatility, StoneX earned $306M. That alone is a 3.4% cash yield on $9B. In the first half of FY2026 it earned $313M, already more than the entire prior year. If the second half simply holds the first-half pace, FY2026 net income clears $600M, a 6.5% to 7% cash yield on today’s price, with the business still growing the underlying client base. On a trailing-twelve-month basis StoneX is already earning close to $500M, a yield in the mid-5s. Put a normalized mid-cycle number somewhere between the FY2025 trough and the FY2026 run-rate, call it $450M to $550M, and you are buying a double-digit grower with a 20%-plus ROE at a roughly 5% to 6% FCF yield and around 15x forward earnings.

That is cheap for what it is, and the DCF math agrees. My updated model discounts FCF to equity at the cost of equity, because StoneX’s balance sheet leverage is client float, not corporate debt, so a normal enterprise-value bridge would mislead. The base case values the equity at about $15B, near 65% above the $9B the market is paying, which works out to $190.

Two inputs do the heavy lifting.

The first is the discount rate, a cost of equity of 7% that reflects a low beta for a business whose earnings actually rise in stress. The second is ROE: I now model a through-cycle ROE of about 18%, still well below the 22% to 26% StoneX printed in the last two quarters, which means it has to retain less capital to fund the same growth and more of each year’s earnings flows to owners. Both are defensible but sit at the optimistic end. Lower the growth, normalize ROE, and lift the discount rate, and you get the bear case, about $80, which I take seriously and lay out below.

The reinvestment point ties it together. StoneX retains almost all of its earnings rather than paying a dividend, and it puts that capital to work at a 15%-plus ROE, recently far higher. So the portion of free cash flow that isn’t distributed isn’t lost, it compounds inside the business at a high rate of return and shows up later as a bigger earnings base and buybacks. A 5% to 7% cash yield that is mostly retained and reinvested at 20% is a better deal than a 5% yield paid out in full. The market is treating StoneX’s cash like low-quality trading profit. It looks a lot more like owner earnings compounding at a high rate behind a cheap price.

You can view the model here.

Scenario analysis: discount rate and growth

The base case rests on two judgement calls, the cost of equity and the long-run growth rate, and the table below shows how much they move the answer. Hold growth at a steady 4% to 5% and lift the discount rate from my 7% toward a more conventional 9%, and fair value falls from about $190 to roughly $99 to $111. Push the discount rate to 10% and you are down near $82 to $88.

Terminal growth swings it just as hard. At a 9% cost of equity, moving long-run growth from 3% to 5% takes fair value from about $91 to $111. The wide spread is the honest message. Because more than 80% of the value sits in the terminal, StoneX is worth a great deal if you accept a low discount rate for a counter-cyclical earner, and merely fair if you hold a more cautious view. The bear case at $80 is the cautious corner of this same grid.

Financials and the DCF

Step back from the quarter-to-quarter noise, and the long arc is what matters. Net operating revenue compounded from $868M in FY2020 to $2.05B in FY2025, that’s a CAGR of 18.8%, through a pandemic, a rate shock, a commodity spike, and stretches of calm. Pre-tax operating margin sat near 20% in FY2025 and is widening as the cost base scales. ROE has run between the mid-teens and the mid-20s, above the 15% target that management is paid to hit. Book value per share has compounded as earnings are retained.

This is the financial signature of a quality compounder, and a here-today trading desk never looks like this.

The DCF builds straight off that record. I model net operating revenue growing at the segment level, around 13% near-term tapering toward 5% in the out years, which is below StoneX’s own five-year history and well below the 47% to 70% growth of the last two quarters. I lift pre-tax margin gradually from 20% toward the mid-20s, grounded in the operating leverage already visible as adjusted EBITDA more than doubled on a 70% revenue gain. I model a through-cycle ROE of 18%, above the FY2025 level but well under the 22% to 26% of the last two quarters, with long-run growth around 4.7%. Tax sits at 25%. On those inputs, free cash flow to equity discounts back to about $15B of equity value, or roughly $190 a share.

Two caveats keep me honest about that number. First, more than 80% of the modelled value sits in the terminal value, which is what happens when you discount a growing stream at a rate close to its growth rate. That makes the base case sensitive to the discount rate and the long-run growth assumption. Second, the gap to the bear case is wide. Hold growth lower, assume no further margin expansion, and use a more conventional discount rate, and the same model produces about $80. The truth is a range, and the width of that range is itself a fact about the stock: at today’s $116 you are paying close to the midpoint of a fundamentally justified band, not a screaming discount to a precise target.

The bear case

Start with the obvious. A large part of the last two quarters is volatility. A 26.5% ROE quarter is not the run-rate. If global markets calm down, if rate cuts shrink the interest StoneX earns on client float, and if commodity volatility fades, net operating revenue growth slows hard and margins stop expanding. The bear DCF that produces $80 isn’t a stretch; it’s just the same business modelled without the tailwind, and it sits roughly 30% below today’s price. Buying a cyclical near a volatility peak is how people lose money even on good companies.

Then there’s valuation history. As recently as 2024 this was a sub-$50 stock trading at high-single-digit earnings. It has more than doubled in a year and now trades around 21x forward earnings.

The easy re-rating, from forgotten micro-cap to recognized compounder, has already happened. The next leg has to come from earnings, not from the multiple, and earnings are the part most exposed to the volatility cycle.

The acquisition cadence cuts both ways. StoneX is a serial acquirer, and RJO plus the earlier Benchmark deal add real integration risk. A reasonable skeptic would point out that a flurry of deals can flatter headline growth while the organic trend underneath softens, and that StoneX’s business is opaque enough that it’s hard to fully separate the two. The $100M benefit target is management’s number, not a delivered result. If integration drags or the acquired books don’t cross-sell as hoped, the scale story stalls.

The deepest risk is structural to what StoneX is. This is a clearing and execution firm that stands between clients and markets, which means it carries the risk of client defaults, trading errors, and operational or compliance failures. A single large clearing blow-up, a rogue position, or a regulatory sanction at a futures commission merchant can erase a year of profit or worse. The 2022 nickel episode at the LME and the recurring history of FCM failures, from MF Global in 2011 to Peregrine the year after, are reminders that the toll-booth model has a tail. StoneX manages this risk well and has for years, but the tail does not go away because it has been quiet.

Net it out and the bear case is coherent: a volatility-juiced cyclical, re-rated after a double, growing partly by acquisition, carrying a small but real chance of a clearing shock, priced at a level that already assumes the good times continue. That is a genuine argument, and it’s why I treat $80 as the floor of the range rather than a tail scenario.

Variant perception

So where do I disagree with the market, and why am I on the bull side despite a fair bear case?

The mispricing lives in how the business is read rather than in the numbers themselves. The market still files StoneX under a thin-margin commodity broker because of the $131B gross line and the swings in quarterly results. That framing cuts a strange way on the screen. StoneX trades around 21 times forward earnings and 25 times trailing, a clear premium to the roughly 12 times the diversified-financials sector carries, so on a peer-multiple lens it looks expensive. That is the trap. A peer multiple is the wrong tool for a 20%-plus ROE compounder that reinvests at those rates, and on cash flow even today’s premium understates what the business earns. What they’re actually looking at is a capital-light intermediary that has compounded its real top line at roughly 19% a year for five years, earns a 20%-plus margin and a high-teens-to-mid-20s ROE, retains and reinvests at those rates, and sits on a structural tailwind as banks keep retreating from the middle market and the industry consolidates around scale players like StoneX.

The volatility that the market treats as a bug is closer to a feature once you hold the position for years rather than quarters. Across a full cycle StoneX grows in the calm and prints in the chaos, a return profile worth paying up for. And the cash flow is the proof that cuts through the framing argument. A business earning north of $600M on the current run-rate against a $9B price, mostly retained and reinvested at a 20% return, is not priced like the market understands what it owns.

That’s the variant view in one line: StoneX is a quality compounder wearing the costume of a commodity trader, and the cash flow against the price is the receipt.

Verdict

At about $116, StoneX is a buy for anyone willing to underwrite mid-cycle earnings power and treat the volatility as an option rather than the whole thesis. You are paying 21x forward earnings and a mid-single-digit FCF yield for a double-digit compounder with a 20%-plus ROE, a structural tailwind, and a balance sheet of client float rather than real debt.
